name: AntiSlop

status.note: No changes by its author since January 9, 2026; only automated dependency updates since. The latest published version is 0.3.0.

summary: A small Rust CLI that scans source code for signs of unfinished AI-generated work: `TODO` placeholders, “for now” deferrals, “should work” hedging in comments, empty stubs and placeholder data.
intro: AntiSlop is a one-person project published on crates.io (where docs.rs hosts its API docs) and npm. It doesn’t look for bugs or style problems, which it leaves to ESLint, Clippy and the like; it looks for code that admits it isn’t finished. Its categories are placeholders (`TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK`), deferrals (“for now”, “temporary fix”), hedging (“hopefully”, “should work”), stubs (empty functions, `todo!()`, `pass`), error suppression (`unwrap()`, `@ts-ignore`) and redundant comments. Most of these are phrases in comments, so in practice it is a word-list checker for code comments plus a few syntax checks.

It matches regular expressions and, for about a dozen languages, uses tree-sitter grammars to find comments and function bodies; Kotlin, PHP, Swift and a few others are regex-only. Three profiles control how much it reports: the default `core` checks only placeholders and stubs, `antislop-standard` adds deferrals, hedging and dummy data, and `antislop-strict` adds nitpicks. Each run prints findings with a severity and a “sloppy score”, and `--json` produces machine-readable output. Custom patterns go in an `antislop.toml` file. The repository also includes a GitHub Action, a pre-commit hook, a Docker image and a VS Code extension.
strengths: Catches leftover `TODO`s, stubs and hedging comments that compile and pass ordinary linters
Fast, a single binary installed from Cargo, npm, Homebrew or a shell script, with no configuration needed
Custom patterns are a few lines of TOML
limits: Mostly phrase matching: “for now” or “should work” in a legitimate comment is reported too, despite the README’s “zero false positives” claim for the default profile
The checks find unfinished code whoever wrote it; a `TODO` or a hedge is not proof that an AI was involved
A personal project (16 GitHub stars) that its author stopped changing in January 2026; the changelog lists a 1.0.0 that was never published

story: Stefan Wiest, who describes his work as AI research and multi-agent systems, created AntiSlop on December 31, 2025 and published version 0.2.1 to crates.io and npm the next day. Over the following week he added hedging patterns, filename checks for AI-generated duplicate files, the profiles and a “hygiene survey” that detects which linters, formatters and CI a project already uses, releasing 0.3.0 on January 7, 2026. After a last round of documentation changes on January 9 the project went quiet.

choices.choice: Stay out of what standard linters catch
choices.why: The README’s rule is that anything ESLint or Clippy flags by default is not AntiSlop’s job, so it can focus on unfinished intent.

choices.choice: Regex plus tree-sitter, with optional languages
choices.why: Regex alone is fastest; tree-sitter grammars make comment and stub detection accurate, and Cargo features let users build in only the languages they need.

timeline.text: January 9: last change by the author
